title: UNIT 1: RELATIONS AND FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ Relation → a pairing or connection between objects or numbers.

✓ Function → a special type of relation in which each input has exactly one output.

title: 1.1.1 REVISION OF PATTERNS
notes:
✓ Pattern → a regular or repeated arrangement that follows a predictable rule.

◆ Even-number pattern → 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
◆ Odd-number pattern → 1, 3, 5, 7, ...

✓ Arithmetic pattern → each term is obtained by adding or subtracting a constant number.
Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... → add 2.

✓ Geometric pattern → each term is obtained by multiplying or dividing by a constant number.
Example: 2, 4, 8, 16, ... → multiply by 2.

Patterns can be represented using tables, diagrams, sequences, or algebraic expressions.

title: 1.1.2 CARTESIAN COORDINATE SYSTEM
notes:
✓ Cartesian coordinate system → a plane formed by two perpendicular number lines: the x-axis and y-axis.

✓ Origin → intersection of the two axes: (0, 0).

✓ Ordered pair → (x, y), where x is the abscissa and y is the ordinate.

◆ x-coordinate → horizontal position.
◆ y-coordinate → vertical position.

◆ Four quadrants:
I → (+,+)
II → (−,+)
III → (−,−)
IV → (+,−)

Example: P(3, 2) has x-coordinate 3 and y-coordinate 2.

title: 1.1.3 BASIC CONCEPTS OF RELATIONS
notes:
✓ Relation → a set of ordered pairs.

A relation can connect elements of two sets or relate real numbers using a rule.

Example:
R = {(1,2), (2,4), (3,6)}

Each ordered pair is written as (x, y), where x is the first component and y is the second component.

✓ Order matters: (2,3) and (3,2) represent different ordered pairs.

◆ Relations may be represented by:
• Ordered pairs
• Tables
• Arrow diagrams
• Equations
• Graphs.

title: DOMAIN AND RANGE OF A RELATION
1.1.4 GRAPHS OF RELATIONS
notes:
A relation can be represented graphically by plotting its ordered pairs on the Cartesian plane.

✓ To graph a relation:
◆ Choose values of x.
◆ Find corresponding y-values.
◆ Plot (x,y).
◆ Join or shade the required points/region.

✓ For inequalities:
◆ ≤ or ≥ → solid boundary line.
◆ < or > → broken/dashed boundary line.

Test a point from a region to determine which side satisfies the inequality.

title: GRAPHING RELATIONS WITH INEQUALITIES
notes:
For a relation involving an inequality, first draw the boundary equation.

◆ ≤ or ≥ → include the boundary → solid line.
◆ < or > → exclude the boundary → broken line.

Example:
y ≤ x + 2

Draw y = x + 2 using a solid line, then shade the region below the line because the inequality is ≤.

For two inequalities, the required graph is the common/intersection region satisfying both conditions.

title: 1.2 FUNCTIONS: THE NOTION OF FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Function → a relation in which no two distinct ordered pairs have the same first element with different second elements.

In simple terms → every input has exactly ONE output.

Example:
f = {(1,5), (2,6), (3,7)} → function.

{(1,5), (1,8)} → not a function because input 1 has two different outputs.

A function can be written as:
f: A → B

or
f(x) = expression.

title: TESTING WHETHER A RELATION IS A FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Ordered-pair test:
If the same x-value is paired with two different y-values, it is NOT a function.

Example:
{(1,2), (2,3), (3,4)} → function.

{(1,2), (1,5), (3,4)} → not a function.

✓ Vertical line test → a graph represents a function if every vertical line intersects the graph at most once.

✓ One input → exactly one output.

title: DOMAIN, CODOMAIN & RANGE OF A FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Domain → all permitted input values of a function.

✓ Codomain → the set into which the function maps its inputs.

✓ Range → the actual output values produced by the function.

✓ Important:
Range ⊆ Codomain.

Example:
f(x) = x², f: R → R
Domain = R
Codomain = R
Range = {y ∈ R : y ≥ 0}

Function notation f(x) means the value of the function at x.

title: EVALUATING A FUNCTION
notes:
✓ To evaluate f(a), substitute x = a into the function.

Example:
f(x) = x + 5

f(4) = 4 + 5 = 9

Therefore, the image of 4 is 9.

Always check the domain before evaluating a function.

For square-root functions, the expression inside the radical must be non-negative.

title: TYPES OF FUNCTIONS
notes:
◆ One-to-one / Injective → different inputs have different outputs.

If f(x₁) = f(x₂), then x₁ = x₂.

◆ Onto / Surjective → every element of the codomain has at least one pre-image in the domain.

◆ Bijective → both one-to-one and onto.

Bijective function → every codomain element corresponds to exactly one domain element.

A function may be injective, surjective, both, or neither.

title: ONE-TO-ONE, ONTO & BIJECTIVE
notes:
✓ Injective → no two different inputs map to the same output.

✓ Surjective → every element in the codomain is reached.

✓ Bijective → injective + surjective.

Example:
f: R → R, f(x) = x + 1

Different x-values give different outputs, and every real number is reached.
Therefore f is bijective.

Bijective functions have a unique inverse relationship.

title: COMBINATION OF FUNCTIONS
notes:
Two functions can be combined using addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

◆ Sum:
(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)

◆ Difference:
(f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x)

◆ Product:
(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)

◆ Quotient:
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x), where g(x) ≠ 0.

Example:
f(x)=2x+1, g(x)=x−1
(f+g)(x)=3x.

title: DOMAIN OF COMBINED FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ For f+g, f−g and fg:
Domain = common values in the domains of f and g.

✓ For f/g:
Domain = common domain values where g(x) ≠ 0.

Example:
f(x)=√x → domain x ≥ 0

g(x)=√(4−x²) → domain −2 ≤ x ≤ 2

Common domain → 0 ≤ x ≤ 2.

For f/g, also exclude values where g(x)=0.

title: GRAPHS OF FUNCTIONS
notes:
✓ The graph of f is the set of all ordered pairs:
{(x, f(x)) : x belongs to the domain}.

✓ To sketch a graph:
◆ Select x-values.
◆ Calculate f(x).
◆ Create ordered pairs.
◆ Plot the points.
◆ Join them according to the type of function.

Graphs connect algebraic expressions with geometric representations.

title: LINEAR FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Linear function:
f(x) = ax + b, a ≠ 0.

◆ a → slope
◆ b → y-intercept

✓ Graph → straight line.

◆ a > 0 → increasing.
◆ a < 0 → decreasing.
◆ a = 0 → constant function.

Example:
f(x)=2x+1
Slope = 2
Y-intercept = (0,1).

title: SLOPE & INTERCEPTS
notes:
In y = ax + b:

◆ a → slope/steepness of the line.
◆ b → y-intercept.

✓ x-intercept → put y = 0 and solve for x.

✓ y-intercept → put x = 0.

Example:
y = 3x − 6

x-intercept:
0 = 3x − 6 → x = 2 → (2,0)

y-intercept:
y = −6 → (0,−6).

title: CONSTANT FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Constant function:
f(x) = b

It is a special case of f(x)=ax+b when a=0.

✓ Graph → horizontal straight line.

Example:
f(x)=2

For every x:
f(x)=2.

Domain → all real numbers.
Range → {2}.

The output remains unchanged regardless of the input.

title: QUADRATIC FUNCTION
notes:
✓ Quadratic function:
f(x) = ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0.

◆ a → leading coefficient.
✓ Graph → parabola.
◆ Parabola has a vertex and axis of symmetry.

◆ If a > 0 → opens upward → minimum value.
◆ If a < 0 → opens downward → maximum value.

Example:
f(x)=x²−4x+3.

title: BASIC PARABOLA: y = ax²
notes:
For y = ax²:

◆ Vertex = (0,0).
◆ Axis of symmetry = x = 0.
◆ Domain = all real numbers.

◆ If a > 0 → opens upward and range is y ≥ 0.

◆ If a < 0 → opens downward and range is y ≤ 0.

◆ Larger |a| → narrower/steeper parabola.
◆ Smaller |a| → wider parabola.

Example:
y=2x² opens upward and is narrower than y=x².

title: GRAPH OF y = ax² + c
notes:
In y = ax² + c, the parabola y=ax² is shifted vertically by c units.

◆ Vertex = (0,c).
◆ Axis of symmetry = x=0.
◆ Domain = R.

◆ If a > 0:
Range → y ≥ c.

◆ If a < 0:
Range → y ≤ c.

Example:
y=x²+2 → y=x² shifted upward by 2 units.

title: HORIZONTAL SHIFT OF A PARABOLA
notes:
✓ Function:
y = a(x−k)²

The graph of y=ax² is shifted horizontally.

◆ Vertex = (k,0).
◆ Axis of symmetry = x=k.

Example:
y=(x−3)²
→ y=x² shifted 3 units to the right.

Example:
y=(x+2)²
→ y=x² shifted 2 units to the left.

✓ General translated parabola:
y = a(x−k)² + m

◆ Vertex = (k,m).
◆ Axis of symmetry = x=k.

◆ If a > 0 → opens upward.
◆ If a < 0 → opens downward.

Example:
y=(x−3)²+2
Vertex = (3,2)
Axis of symmetry = x=3.

This form makes the position and direction of the parabola easy to identify.

title: COMPLETING THE SQUARE
notes:
✓ A quadratic function can be rewritten in vertex form using completing the square.

◆ General form:
y=ax²+bx+c

◆ Vertex form:
y=a(x−h)²+k

The textbook uses completing the square to identify the vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts and shape of a general quadratic graph.

Example:
y=x²+6x+11
= (x+3)²+2

Vertex = (−3,2)
Axis of symmetry = x=−3.

title: VERTEX, AXIS & INTERCEPTS
notes:
✓ For y=a(x−h)²+k:

◆ Vertex = (h,k).
◆ Axis of symmetry = x=h.
◆ If a>0 → minimum at the vertex.
◆ If a<0 → maximum at the vertex.

✓ x-intercepts → set y=0 and solve.
✓ y-intercept → set x=0.

These features allow a parabola to be sketched accurately.

title: MAXIMUM & MINIMUM VALUES
notes:
✓ A quadratic parabola has one extreme value at its vertex.

◆ If a > 0 → parabola opens upward → vertex gives the minimum value.

◆ If a < 0 → parabola opens downward → vertex gives the maximum value.

Example:
f(x)=−(x−3)²+1
Vertex = (3,1)
Therefore maximum value = 1.

Range → y ≤ 1.

title: UNIT 1 QUICK FORMULA SUMMARY
notes:
✓ Relation → set of ordered pairs.

✓ Domain → first components/input values.

✓ Range → second components/output values.

✓ Function → every input has exactly one output.

✓ Linear:
f(x)=ax+b
Slope=a
Y-intercept=(0,b)

✓ Quadratic:
f(x)=ax²+bx+c, a≠0

✓ Vertex form:
f(x)=a(x−h)²+k

Vertex=(h,k)

Axis of symmetry: x=h

✓ Vertex of ax²+bx+c:
x = −b/(2a)

✓ Function operations:
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)

(f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x)

(fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)

(f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x), g(x)≠0.
